I don't give a shit about Halloween. Why? Because I have to work, every year, until midnight. So fuck you and your Halloween parties and your trick or treaters and your costumes and your goddamn candy, fucking whatever, I'll buy a bag of Snickers next week at 50% off.

But the buildup to Halloween, the multimedia blitzkrieg of advertising and discussion, is something that even I can not resist, and it puts me in the mood for creepy and scary and Halloween night I like to have a drink, smoke a joint, and play whatever the current 'scariest game' is.

Three years ago it was Amnesia (I know the game is older but my rig sucked). Two years ago was Outlast. Last year I think I replayed Condemned (too much drinking on that one, fuzzy memories). Usually I get about an hour or two into it and quit like a pussy and watch cartoons all night.

This year I'm going with Spirits of Xanadu. Never heard of it? Not a big surprise. It's the only original IP put out by Night Dive Studios, the developer responsible for many of the recent (and excellent) old PC game rereleases like System Shock, Noctropolis, all the Freddy Fish games, Strife, Deadlock, etc. The game didn't make a big splash, in fact I only found it by accident.

So why opt for Spirits of Xanadu over bigger, more obvious titles, primary among them Frictional Games' SOMA? A couple reasons. First, Spirits is on sale for $4.99. Second, I want to give these guys a chance because they are clearly pretty cool dudes. Third, I'm still a little pissed that Machine for Pigs (Frictional's previous release which they published but did not develop) let me down. Fourth, if Spirits of Xanadu happens to suck I will have some backup games to play.

Primary among them, for no other reason than I have not played it before and it looks crazy, is Capsule. Wtf is Capsule, you ask? I have no fucking idea, really; the description is vague and the gameplay images bizarre, but I know one thing for certain: it is on sale for $0.99 and I am willing to give it a shot. The description reads simply: "Capsule is a single-player survival game played entirely through a radar interface. " You get my dollar for that line alone, at least when I see that the Steam reviews are Very Positive. There is a big warning in caps midway through the description and it ends with this:

Capsule is a short game, approximately 2 hours for most players. Capsule is not a game for everyone; if you are claustrophobic, misophonic, and/or have anxiety or triggers related to asphyxiation and/or darkness Capsule may not be a good game for you.

I am fucking in. Add to that the game was developed by two dudes (or a dude and a chick maybe) and I can't say no.

But let's face it, Capsule might also suck, and if nothing else 2 hours might not be enough scary for me. If this is the case I have Deadnaut to fall back on. Deadnaut is another extremely experimental game, this one from Australian indie developer Screwfly Studios. Screwfly made the very impressive (and underrated) Zafehouse Diaries game a couple years back where you command (or try to command) a group of random zombipocalypse survivors that probably hate each other for all types of stupid reasons. Zafehouse Diaries is the first game I've played where procedurally generated characters could be racist, sexist, or homophobic and these characteristics actually mattered (and were presented maturely without a whole lot of unnecessary cultural criticism and commentary): based on the characters' relationships they work better or worse with each other, and fights can break out between characters that hate each other. On the backdrop of surviving and escaping a zombie infested town I found this to be pretty compelling, so I'd suggest checking out the demo for Zafehouse Diaries if you have never heard of it. The game interface is a little weird and there aren't really any graphics so, yknow, it's probably best to give it a shot before committing to it. Here's the link for the demo.

Deadnaut applies this social dynamic to a very different environment: you command a group of misfit explorers tasked with investigating derelict space ships left over from long dead alien civilizations. The game is a bit like if original Syndicate (or the more recent Satellite Reign) had a baby with The Escapists, with a dash of old FMV game Mission Critical thrown in and then someone forgot to finish the graphics. All the action takes place on a little view window that takes up maybe 1/3 of the screen, and is composed solely of simple 3d objects and little symbols that move around (for your team). The audio is mostly humming, creepy ambient noise and static; the team dialog is shown in text. And yet, from these humble pieces is wrought one of the most tense, creepy experiences I've had in a long time. Basically, you send your team onto the first ship (each randomly generated campaign consists of 4 procedurally generated ships of escalating difficulty) totally blind, not knowing what they'll find, poorly equipped and untested. On that first ship they will encounter the 'threats,' which can range from possessed bodies to hell spawn to aliens with machine guns (also procedurally generated). If you manage to survive the first ship you can use the knowledge gained from your encounters to equip your team more efficiently for their next excursion. The game oozes tension and atmosphere and is so unique that it requires a whole lot of space to even describe, so just check out the demo if any of this sounds cool, it's available for Windows, OSX and Linux. Here's a link to the demo.

In the unlikely event that I dislike Xanadu and Capsule AND somehow complete a campaign of Deadnaut (which can take less than 2 hrs if you're very lucky), what then, eh? Here's what then: goddamn System Shock Enhanced. System Shock, with its ubiquitous AI villain SHODAN, is one of the greatest games ever made, developed by one of the best developers that ever existed (Looking Glass Studios, who brought us little games like Ultima Underworld and Thief, games that have never been outdone in their respective genres even decades after their release). In System Shock you are an anonymous hacker, grafted with cybernetics, that awakens on a space station after six months of healing coma to find SHODAN, the station AI has gone mad, killed or mutated everyone, and is planning on conquering and/or destroying earth. SHODAN is one of the best villains in all vidya, especially impressive considering the age of the game and the formulaic simplicity of many of its peers from the same time. Unlike most traditional vidya villains SHODAN is constantly taunting and messing with you, threatening you directly, and it is creepy as hell. System Shock is genuinely scary and tense without the need for any supernatural nonsense, and though the game systems are relatively complicated (it is a first person RPG with some pretty intense movement controls, though everything is easily mappable with the new Enhanced version) and the game might seem to be impenetrable at first, players that put the effort in will be rewarded with what might be the best cyberpunk RPG of forever. Fucking SHODAN, man, just listen to this random recording you find (no spoilers): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wQtZPNjc2gY

So there is no way to go wrong with System Shock Enhanced, and my Halloween will conclude there (assuming it doesn't end with inebriated failure hours earlier), but for $2.49 you can also get the 1999 sequel System Shock 2, so why the hell wouldn't you do that? The best part is, you don't even need to BEAT the original game to enjoy the sequel, though you should at least play through the first level or so. System Shock 2 is a much more modern (ie, 3D accelerated) game and arguably much more approachable, though it still retains RPG elements and a pretty high difficulty and the graphics are pretty rough from a modern perspective. It is also IMMEDIATELY terrifying, and the enemies in the game (and the several mindblowing reveals that occur) are some of the best of any medium. There are several mods that can make the experience more 'modern' (widescreen resolution fixes and model complexity upgrades, etc) but not strictly speaking necessary.

So tallying all these games up brings us to $21.45, less than half the price of a new quote AAA unquote game, about the price of a new small studio game or three drinks at a bar here in the US. A fine investment for a spoopy evening at home.
